pharm: Topical alpha-hydroxy acid used as a chemical exfoliant and keratolytic in skin care and dermatological peels for photoageing, acne, hyperpigmentation, and keratinisation disorders.
quick: Topical: leave-on products typically 5-15% applied once or twice daily; chemical peels 20-70% applied by a professional for minutes then neutralised
Topical use; not related to meals
Topical use considered low systemic absorption; generally regarded as acceptable, but data are limited
Topical use with minimal systemic absorption; avoid application to the breast/nipple area
Avoid alcohol-based products that increase irritation on treated skin
Skin tolerance (irritation, redness, peeling), photosensitivity, post-peel healing
summary: Glycolic acid is the smallest alpha-hydroxy acid (derived from sugar cane) used topically as a keratolytic and chemical exfoliant. At low concentrations in leave-on cosmetic and dermatological products it smooths and exfoliates the skin, improving photoageing, fine lines, hyperpigmentation, acne, and rough/keratotic skin; at higher concentrations it is used for superficial-to-medium chemical peels performed by trained professionals and neutralised after a set time. It increases skin sensitivity to the sun, so daily sunscreen is essential. The main adverse effects are local irritation, redness, stinging, peeling, and, with stronger peels, risk of burns, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and scarring if misused.
indications: Exfoliation and improvement of photoaged skin (fine lines, rough texture, dullness)
Hyperpigmentation, melasma, and uneven skin tone (often combined with other agents)
Hyperkeratotic conditions (e.g., keratosis pilaris, ichthyosis-type dry skin)

dosage.d: Approximately 5-15% applied to clean dry skin once or twice daily, starting at lower frequency to build tolerance
dosage.n: Avoid eyes, lips, and mucous membranes; use sunscreen

dosage.d: 20-70% solution applied by a trained clinician for a defined contact time (typically minutes), then neutralised/rinsed
dosage.n: Must be neutralised; performed under professional supervision

dosage.d: Lower concentration applied every other day initially, increasing as tolerated

admin: Apply to clean, dry skin; avoid the eyes, lips, nostrils, and broken or irritated skin
Introduce gradually (lower strength, less frequent use) to build tolerance and limit irritation
Use a broad-spectrum sunscreen daily and limit sun exposure, as glycolic acid increases photosensitivity
For professional peels, neutralise/rinse after the prescribed contact time and follow post-peel skin care
Do not combine aggressively with other strong actives (e.g., retinoids, other acids) without guidance
moa: Glycolic acid is an alpha-hydroxy acid that reduces corneocyte cohesion in the stratum corneum by interfering with the ionic bonds and intercellular adhesion between keratinocytes, promoting desquamation (exfoliation) of the outer skin layers. This thins the stratum corneum, smooths skin texture, and stimulates turnover; with repeated or higher-concentration use it can promote epidermal renewal and dermal remodelling (increased glycosaminoglycans and collagen), improving the appearance of photoaged and hyperpigmented skin.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to glycolic acid or product components
Application to broken, inflamed, infected, or sunburned skin
relative: Very sensitive or atopic skin (higher irritation risk)
Recent use of isotretinoin or aggressive resurfacing (delay peels)
Active herpes simplex in the treatment area (procedural peels)
History of keloid/abnormal scarring or post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (caution with deeper peels)
monitor: Local irritation, redness, stinging, and peeling
Signs of excessive injury (blistering, prolonged erythema) with peels

preg: Topical glycolic acid has minimal systemic absorption and is generally regarded as acceptable during pregnancy, though robust data are limited. Use low-concentration leave-on products as needed and discuss professional peels with a clinician; avoid combining with agents contraindicated in pregnancy.
lact: Systemic absorption from topical application is minimal, so use during breastfeeding is generally considered acceptable. Avoid applying directly to the breast or nipple area to prevent infant ingestion.
renal: Not applicable - topical glycolic acid has negligible systemic absorption and no renal dose considerations.
hepatic: Not applicable - topical glycolic acid has negligible systemic absorption and no hepatic dose considerations.

major: None systemically significant for topical use
moderate: Concurrent topical retinoids, benzoyl peroxide, other acids, or physical exfoliants - additive irritation; introduce cautiously
Recent or concurrent skin resurfacing/laser/isotretinoin - increased irritation and injury risk
minor: Alcohol-based or fragranced topical products may increase irritation on treated skin
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol-containing topical products on treated areas as they increase irritation and dryness.
interactions.diagnostics: No laboratory monitoring required; assessment is clinical (skin tolerance and response).

common: Mild burning, stinging, or tingling on application
serious: Chemical burns or blistering with high concentrations or prolonged contact
Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, especially in darker skin
Scarring with misuse of deeper peels
emergency: Severe chemical burn with blistering and pain (professional peel mishap)
Signs of secondary skin infection (spreading redness, pus, fever)

monitoring: Skin tolerance: degree of irritation, redness, and peeling, adjusting concentration/frequency accordingly
Photosensitivity and adequacy of sun protection
Post-peel healing and any pigment changes (clinical follow-up for procedural peels)
Signs of overuse or chemical burn
counsel: Apply to clean dry skin and avoid your eyes, lips, and nostrils; some tingling or mild stinging is normal
Start slowly (lower strength, every other day) and build up to limit irritation
Use sunscreen every day - this product makes your skin more sensitive to the sun, and continue sun protection for at least a week after a peel
Do not pick or peel flaking skin, and avoid combining with other strong acids or retinoids unless advised
Stop and seek advice if you get severe burning, blistering, prolonged redness, or darkening of the skin
pk: Exfoliating effect develops over days of use; peel effects visible within days after the procedure
Skin texture and tone improvements build over weeks of regular use
Not applicable - negligible systemic absorption from topical use
Effects maintained with continued use; peels last weeks before repeat treatment
Store at room temperature, tightly closed, away from heat and direct light; keep out of reach of children
pearls: Not an FDA-approved drug product - glycolic acid is used as a cosmetic/dermatological alpha-hydroxy acid and in professional chemical peels; this entry follows cosmetic-ingredient and dermatology guidance (EU cosmetic regulation, BNF/derm references)
Concentration and pH determine strength: low % leave-on for daily care, high % (20-70%) for professional peels that MUST be neutralised
Increases photosensitivity - daily broad-spectrum sunscreen is essential
Higher risk of post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in darker skin types; use cautiously and at lower strengths
Introduce gradually and avoid stacking with other strong actives (retinoids, other acids) to limit irritation
missed: For leave-on products, if you miss an application simply resume your usual routine at the next scheduled time - there is no need to apply extra. Consistency over time matters more than any single application.
overdose: Excessive topical use or overly long peel contact can cause chemical burns, blistering, severe irritation, and pigment changes rather than systemic toxicity. Remove/neutralise the product, rinse thoroughly with water, soothe and protect the skin, and seek medical/dermatological care for significant burns or blistering. Accidental ingestion of concentrated solutions can cause mucosal/GI corrosion - seek emergency care.
